submissions.rationale: The claim asserts that FLT3 D835Y predicts sensitivity/response to a therapy list dominated by type II FLT3 inhibitors (quizartinib, sorafenib, ponatinib, linifanib, KW2449, R406, AGS324) plus the type I agents sunitinib and AG1295. The one full-text paper I was able to read (Smith et al., Leukemia 2015, PMID 26108694) systematically profiled every reported D835 substitution in Ba/F3 FLT3-ITD cells against quizartinib, sorafenib, ponatinib, PLX3397 and crenolanib. It places D835Y in the most resistant category: D835V/Y/F "cause a high degree of resistance to all type II inhibitors," with a structural rationale (bulky side chain cannot hydrogen-bond S838, sterically incompatible with the short α-helix, shifting equilibrium to the DFG-in active conformation that type II drugs cannot bind). The paper further notes that only highly resistant D835V/Y/F mutations were recovered from patients relapsing on quizartinib, and that D835Y/H emerged at sorafenib resistance — i.e., D835Y is a clinical resistance, not sensitivity, marker for these drugs. The single element of the claim that survives is the type I agents: the authors state D835 mutants retain sensitivity to crenolanib and that other type I inhibitors "such as sunitinib, would also retain activity," which is consistent with sunitinib (and, by mechanism class, AG1295) but does not rescue the rest of the list. Because the predominant and explicitly tested therapies are contradicted, I record does_not_support rather than conflicting; the sunitinib quote is included as a supporting partial caveat so curators can see the type I/type II split. Caveat: I had limited actions and read only one primary source, so the record rests on a single (though directly on-point and mechanistically detailed) study; no evidence was located for AGS324, linifanib, R406 or AG1295 against D835Y specifically.

submissions.rationale: The claim asserts CYP2D6 loss-of-function is a therapy-independent prognostic marker of poor outcome in breast cancer. The evidence I read does not support this. A large Swedish cohort of 1,103 tamoxifen-treated early breast cancer patients with 11.4 years median follow-up found no significant association between CYP2D6 activity and recurrence (aHR 1.18, 95% CI 0.92–1.52) or breast cancer mortality (aHR 1.41, 95% CI 0.93–2.13), explicitly reversing the authors' own earlier positive finding (PMID 40600576). A pooled review of 13,001 patients across 29 studies confirmed that poor metabolizers have markedly lower endoxifen concentrations, but that poor-metabolizer status did not influence clinical outcomes in the majority of studies (PMID 28762370). Notably, even in the minority of reports suggesting an effect, the mechanism is impaired bioactivation of tamoxifen to endoxifen — i.e., any association is drug-dependent (predictive of tamoxifen response), not a therapy-independent prognostic effect as the claim is framed with no therapies listed. Residual literature heterogeneity exists, but the best-powered and pooled evidence available here weighs against the claim as stated.
